lessons.description: Use number words to describe small groups of food.

materials.content_text:
We can count objects one at a time. If a plate has one banana and two apples, there are three pieces of fruit on the plate. Touching or pointing to each item once can help you keep your place while counting.

Nico puts four crackers on a plate. He adds one more cracker. Now there are five crackers.

Try it: Draw two circles for two pretend snacks. Add one more circle. How many do you see now?

lessons.description: Clubs are groups where people learn or enjoy an activity together. You can share a favorite and ask someone else what they enjoy.
lessons.name: Finding a Club You Enjoy

materials.content_text:
A school club is a group of people who meet to do something together. A music club might sing or play instruments. A robotics club might design and build small machines. An art club can draw, paint, or make things. Different clubs welcome different interests.

To ask about a preference, say, ‘Which club is your favorite?’ You can answer, ‘My favorite is the art club.’ To talk about one other person, say, ‘Nora likes the music club.’ The verb likes has an s after he, she, or one person’s name.

Try it: Name a club you would enjoy. Tell a partner one activity you could do there. There are many good answers because people enjoy different things.

lessons.description: An invitation tells readers what an activity is, where it happens, and when to arrive.
lessons.name: Reading a Club Invitation

materials.content_text:
Read this original invitation:

‘Come to the Garden Club! We meet on Tuesday at three o’clock beside the school garden. We plant seeds, water vegetables, and learn how plants grow. Bring a small water bottle. Everyone is welcome.’

A useful invitation answers questions such as: What is the group? When does it meet? Where does it meet? What will people do? Read the whole notice first, then look back for the detail you need.

For example, the day is Tuesday and the place is beside the school garden. The notice does not tell us the club leader’s name, so we should not guess it.

Try it: Make a short invitation for a club you invent. Include its name, day, place, and one activity.

lessons.description: Explore how animals live in different habitats.
lessons.name: Animal Homes

materials.content_text:
A habitat is the place where an animal lives and finds things it needs. Different animals live in different habitats. A fish may live in water. A bird may build a nest in a tree. A rabbit may rest in a burrow.

Animals of the same kind can live in different places, and not all birds build the same kind of nest. A habitat includes more than a shelter: animals also need food, water, and space.

Try it: Choose an animal and name a place it can live. What might it need there? Observe animals respectfully and do not disturb their homes.

lessons.description: People do many kinds of work. Use a or an before a singular job name when explaining what someone wants to be.
lessons.name: Exploring Different Jobs

materials.content_text:
A reporter asks questions and shares information. A designer plans how something will look or work. A cartoonist creates drawings that tell ideas or stories. A scientist studies questions about the world. People can have many different interests, and anyone can explore a job that interests them.

Use a before a word that starts with a consonant sound: ‘a reporter’ and ‘a designer.’ Use an before a vowel sound: ‘an artist’ and ‘an astronaut.’ The sound at the beginning of the next word matters.

You can say, ‘I want to be an artist,’ or ‘She wants to be a reporter.’ These are ways to talk about a hope; it is fine for hopes to change.

Try it: Choose a job that interests you. Say one thing a person in that job might do.

After running around the field, Ivo felt parched. His mouth was dry, and he asked for a drink of water. He drank slowly and soon felt better.

materials.content_text:
People enjoy different activities. A learner might play a guitar, make paper shapes, act in a play, or build a small robot. Use like to followed by an action: ‘I like to draw.’ With one other person, use likes to: ‘Rina likes to dance.’

Ask, ‘Do you like to draw?’ Answer, ‘Yes, I do,’ or ‘No, I don’t.’ When asking about one person, say, ‘Does Rina like to dance?’ Answer, ‘Yes, she does,’ or ‘No, she doesn’t.’ After does or doesn’t, use like without an s.

lessons.description: When subjects are joined by or or nor, look carefully at the subject nearest the verb.
lessons.name: Choosing a Verb with Or and Nor

materials.content_text:
Or and nor can join alternative subjects. When both subjects are singular, use a singular verb: ‘Either Mara or Leo is bringing the map.’ The word either introduces the alternatives; is matches the singular subjects.

When one subject is singular and the other is plural, the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject in standard English. Compare ‘Either the teachers or the principal is speaking’ with ‘Either the principal or the teachers are speaking.’ The word closest to the verb changes from principal to teachers.

Try it: Write a sentence with two people joined by or. Find the subject nearest the verb and read the sentence aloud. If a sentence sounds awkward, you can also rewrite it to make the meaning clearer.

lessons.description: Use want to and wants to to describe activities you hope to do. A plan can grow and change as you learn.
lessons.name: Talking About Future Plans

materials.content_text:
You can talk about an activity you hope to do: ‘I want to draw a comic,’ or ‘We want to help animals.’ Use want to with I, you, we, and they. Use wants to with he, she, or one person’s name: ‘Ari wants to explore the sea.’

Ask, ‘What do you want to do?’ A possible answer is, ‘I want to make a short film.’ To ask about one other person, say, ‘What does she want to do?’ After does, use want without an s. Answer, ‘She wants to make a short film.’

Try it: Think of something you would like to learn or do. Finish the sentence, ‘I want to…’ Then ask someone else about their idea. There is no single correct dream.

lessons.description: Some everyday nouns are usually plural. Learn how to talk about one pair or several pairs clearly.
lessons.name: Talking About Pairs

materials.content_text:
Some objects have names that usually appear in the plural, even when we are talking about one item. Examples include scissors, trousers, and binoculars. We normally say, ‘These scissors are sharp,’ not ‘This scissors is sharp.’

To count such objects, use pair. Compare: ‘One pair of scissors is on the desk’ and ‘Two pairs of scissors are on the desk.’ In the first sentence, pair is singular, so the verb is is. In the second, pairs is plural, so the verb is are.

Try it: Look for an object at home or school that has two matching parts. Describe one pair, and then imagine describing two pairs. Some words have other meanings, so choose the form that fits your meaning.

lessons.description: Explore how homes may look different and meet people's needs.
lessons.name: Homes Can Be Different

materials.content_text:
Homes can come in many shapes and sizes. Some people live in an apartment in a building. Some live in a house. Some people move between places, and some share a home with relatives or friends.

What makes a place feel welcoming can be different for each person. A safe place to rest and people who care for one another can be important in many homes. Avoid assuming that everyone has the same rooms, family, or belongings.

Try it: Draw an imaginary place where someone could rest. You do not need to share private details about your own home.

lessons.description: A phrase giving extra information can sit between a subject and its verb. Find the main subject before choosing the verb.
lessons.name: Find the Main Subject

materials.content_text:
The main subject tells us who or what the sentence is mainly about. In ‘The coach, along with the players, is ready,’ the main subject is the coach. The phrase along with the players adds information but does not turn the main subject into the players. Because coach is singular, use is.

Compare: ‘The players, along with the coach, are ready.’ Now players is the main subject, so use are. The expressions together with and as well as can also add information after the main subject.

Try it: Find the main subject in ‘The librarian, together with two volunteers, opens the room.’ Cover the extra phrase for a moment: ‘The librarian opens the room.’ Then bring the phrase back and read the whole sentence.

lessons.description: Read a short original story about two learners and find the ideas stated in the text.
lessons.name: A Story About Future Ideas

materials.content_text:
Read this original story:

During library time, Bea finds a book about sea animals. ‘I want to learn how we can protect the ocean,’ she tells her friend Eli. Bea enjoys observing fish and drawing pictures of them.

Eli has a different idea. He likes making small machines from reused boxes. ‘I want to build a helpful robot,’ he says. Together, they decide to make a display for their class: Bea will draw sea animals, and Eli will build a model boat.

What does Bea want to learn about? The story tells us she wants to learn about protecting the ocean. What does Eli want to build? The story says a helpful robot. Their interests are different, but they can still work together.

Try it: Imagine one more idea for their class display. Explain why it fits the story. Your idea can be different from a classmate’s idea.

lessons.description: Each focuses on members one at a time. Practice choosing singular verbs in clear each and each of sentences.
lessons.name: Using Each and Each Of

materials.content_text:
Each points to the members of a group one by one. In ‘Each learner has a notebook,’ each learner is singular, so has fits. In ‘Each of the learners has a notebook,’ the phrase of the learners names the group, while each remains singular in standard formal agreement.

Compare each with all: ‘Each of the books is labeled’ focuses on the books individually; ‘All of the books are labeled’ uses the plural books as its subject. Both sentences can describe the same group from a different point of view.

Try it: Finish ‘Each of my classmates has…’ with something that makes sense for your class. Then make a new sentence beginning ‘All of my classmates…’ and choose a verb that matches.

lessons.description: Read simple location clues and practice asking where to go.
lessons.name: Ask Where a Place Is

materials.content_text:
Pia wants to return a library book. She asks a helper, ‘Excuse me, where is the library?’ The helper says, ‘Walk straight ahead. The library is next to the park and across from the bakery.’

Pia walks straight ahead. She sees the park on one side and the bakery across the road. The library is beside the park, just as the helper said. Pia thanks the helper and returns her book.

Try it: Use next to, across from, or near to describe a place on a map.

lessons.description: Ask what someone would like and answer politely.
lessons.name: Talk About Food Choices

materials.content_text:
At a class picnic, Jo brings a basket of fruit. ‘Would you like an apple or a banana?’ Jo asks. ‘I’d like an apple, please,’ says Kim. Jo passes her one. ‘Thank you!’ Kim says.

Then Kim asks, ‘Would you like some water?’ Jo answers, ‘Yes, please.’ They sit with their friends and share the fruit. People may choose different foods, so it is helpful to ask and listen.

Try it: Ask a partner, ‘Would you like ___ or ___?’ Then answer, ‘I’d like ___, please.’

lessons.description: Find first, next and last in an easy sequence.
lessons.name: Putting Food Steps in Order

materials.content_text:
Instructions tell us what to do. Words such as first, next, and last can make the order clear.

For a pretend fruit picture, first draw a bowl. Next draw two pieces of fruit inside it. Last color your picture. The steps use drawing; you do not need food or kitchen tools.

Try it: Tell someone the three picture steps in order. Then invent one safe extra detail for your picture.
